data.title: Meta sets $300 price on pocket-sized Muse Charm AI device: report
data.description:
Meta Platforms has set a $300 price on its upcoming AI gadget, Muse Charm, according to The Information.

To drive up consumer interests, Meta is also offering a free, 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon , the report said. Meta pushed back the release of its smartwatch until 2027 to get the Muse Charm on the market before Christmas. Earlier this year, Meta set a goal of selling 10M wearable devices during the second half of 2026 as it pushes into a market led by Apple .

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced Charm during its Connect event in September. Roughly the size of an Apple AirPods case, Charm features an approximately 2-inch OLED touchscreen and built-in 5G connectivity. It expects to begin shipping the devices by early December.

Zuckerberg said Charm brings the company's Muse personal AI agent into a portable device that can be carried on a keychain, in a pocket, or with a wrist strap.

"We pack the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to," he said.

The device includes speakers, microphones, front- and rear-facing cameras, a USB-C port, and a customizable virtual Muse character, including options for its appearance and voice. Charm is designed as a dedicated interface for Muse rather than a smartphone replacement. It can connect to Muse over 5G when Wi-Fi is unavailable and is paired and synchronized through the Muse app on an iPhone or Android device. It also supports music and video playback but does not offer phone or video calling. Charm devices can interact with each other as well.

In addition to the Charm and the upcoming smartwatch, Meta is also working on an AI pendant.

data.title: Why Micron, Broadcom and other AI stocks have given up their gains
Trump nominee to head Millennium Challenge aid agency vows to let data guide decisions
data.description:
Key points:
  • Trump's nominee was former public affairs official at Treasury
  • MCC CEO nominee underscores need for data-driven approach
  • Hulse aims to expand external partnerships

By Andrea Shalal

Elliott Hulse, a former US Treasury official nominated to head the Millennium Challenge Corp (MCC), a US aid agency, on Thursday pledged to ensure that evidence-based data would guide decisions on future projects, if confirmed for the job.

Hulse, an adviser to the US executive director at the International Monetary Fund, served as acting assistant secretary of public affairs at the US Treasury before his nomination as chief executive of MCC. He worked at the World Bank from 2019 to 2025.

MCC had been targeted for closure during the early days of the Trump administration as part of a push to end foreign aid programs by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, but ultimately survived. Its budget, which had been around $900 million, was cut by nearly 11% in fiscal 2026, with further cuts proposed for 2027.

Hulse told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during a confirmation hearing that he would aim to build closer ties with Congress, the agency's board members and expand its external partnerships.

He also underscored the need to accelerate the timeline for approving new projects and not "leaving space for other countries or institutions to fill."

Senator Jacky Rosen, a Democrat, asked if Hulse would safeguard the agency's independence and base his decisions on data, noting that nearly a dozen MCC programs had been canceled under pressure from President Donald Trump's administration since January 2025.

"Certainly, if confirmed, I agree with you. The MCC scorecard should be driving all of its decisions, and I believe that data-driven approach is the right way forward," Hulse said.

The Trump administration has canceled MCC programs in several African countries, including Senegal, Kenya, Malawi and Togo, according to a report by the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. It selected Ecuador, Guatemala and Bolivia for new programs, the report noted.

Pressed by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, top Democrat on the panel, on how MCC could ensure no "sweetheart deals" were made that could benefit someone in the US administration, Hulse reiterated his view that data should be the deciding factor.

"As I've emphasized to your colleague Senator Rosen, if confirmed, the scorecard is going to continue to drive every decision that I make," he said.

MCC awards assistance through a process based on countries' performance on a quantitative "scorecard" of indicators sourced from third-party organizations. To be considered, their per capita gross national income must fall under the World Bank's threshold for beginning negotiations to graduate from assistance, which was $8,105 in fiscal 2027.

Sub-Saharan Africa has been the top MCC recipient region to date, but no African countries were selected in 2025. The Trump administration also added "America First" and "America Returns" categories that CRS said were not authorized by US law.

Since its creation in 2004, MCC has signed 50 agreements for grants with 33 countries worth over $18 billion. Not all have been fully implemented, CRS noted.

data.title: Hedge funds trim AMD stakes in Q3 as two exit entirely
data.description:
Hedge fund activity in Advanced Micro Devices () was tilted toward selling in the third quarter, even as the stock outperformed the broader market.

Out of the six hedge fund-reported AMD positions, two exited their positions entirely, two reduced their holdings, one increased its stake, and one maintained its position, according to the latest 13F filings.

AMD shares gained 13.10% during the third quarter, outperforming the S&P 500's (SP500) 2.25% advance.

Among the notable sellers, Duquesne Family Office, led by Stanley Druckenmiller, exited its 73K AMD share position, while Appaloosa Management, led by David Tepper, sold its entire 198K-share stake during the quarter.

Other investors significantly reduced their exposure. Soros Capital, led by Robert Soros, cut its AMD holdings by approximately 98.5%, from 52K shares to just 798 shares.

Discovery Capital, led by Rob Citrone, reduced its position by 62.5%, bringing its holdings down to 3K shares from 8K.

Glenview Capital, led by Larry Robbins and Mark Horowitz, was the only fund among the five that traded AMD to increase its stake. The firm raised its holdings by approximately 31.2%, to 391K shares from 298K.

Tiger Global, meanwhile, kept its 675K-share AMD position unchanged during the quarter.

data.title: Broad Selloff in Stock Market as Anthropic Starts Trading — Market Talk
data.description:
1441 ET - Anthropic shares trade well above their IPO price, but the rest of the market is selling off with weakness from the neocloud sector to health insurance. UnitedHealth Group slides 4.6% after plunging 10% Wednesday following the government pledge to crack down on Medicare Advantage fraud earlier this week and lawmakers' renewed a call for Medicare for All. Centene, Cigna and Elevance Health are all lower as well. Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all down over 4% as investors continue to worry about financing the AI infrastructure buildout. DJIA is off 1.7%, S&P 500 drops 1.4% and the Nasdaq slides 1.6%. (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

1416 ET - Canadian grocer Metro's post-strike recovery in fiscal 2027 take time rather than come on immediately, says RBC's Irene Nattel. "With return to work as of the 1st day of F27, the key question is the slope of food SSS [same-store sales] recovery in Quebec and associated margin recovery," the analyst says in a note. However, she says that the underlying thesis remains unchanged with an 8%-10% EPS growth framework reaffirmed. "Discount expansion is on track, pharmacy remains a structural growth driver, and capital return discipline is intact," she adds. Because normalization will be gradual, Nattel trims her fiscal 2027 and 2028 EPS estimates by about 4% and lowers her price target by C$4 to C$112.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

1408 ET - Anthropic's IPO is a positive for the tech industry right now, but it isn't a fix-all, tech analyst Luke Lango says. "Don't mistake one blockbuster deal for an all-clear signal," Lango warns. The IPO represents Wall Street betting on a leading frontier lab that is already winning in the AI race. That is very different from bets on debt-heavy neoclouds and riskier corners of the AI industry, Lango says. The IPO doesn't address underlying concerns about increased export controls and supply-chain shortages throughout AI, he says. "The AI capital spigot is still open, but not gushing like it used to," Lango says. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

1359 ET - Anthropic is off to a strong start on the public markets, but could be headed for more volatility, says Ben Barringer, head of tech research at Quilter Cheviot. The company is trading more than 15% higher than the offering price it set last night. However, Barringer says the stock is likely to be volatile over the next few weeks as the initial exuberance wears off. While Anthropic is well positioned, it won't be immune to the industry volatility that has followed the midterm elections, Barringer says. Anthropic's models are still very young and the company has to avoid promoting overregulation that could choke growth, he says. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

Andrew Clinton is CEO of Clinton Investment Management. "New Tax Measures Could Add to Munis' Appeal — Market Talk," at 11:36 a.m ET and "Muni Investors Tricked by Rates Volatility — Market Talk," at 11:46 a.m ET on Nov. 18 incorrectly identified the firm as Clinton Asset Management.

1356 ET - Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate jumped 17 basis points to 7.28% this week, reversing four weeks of declines. Realtor.com Senior Economist Anthony Smith says hot inflation data and the persistence of the conflict in Iran will likely place upward pressure on bond yields and borrowing costs. The debate has now shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves. That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in rates through mid-October took its toll. The supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1355 ET - Anthropic's big IPO could help boost confidence at a rough time for the tech industry, Yorkville Ives analysts say. The IPO sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure infrastructure, as Anthropic is a central player in AI buildout, they say. The analysts project that capital expenditures over the next few years in the AI industry will hit $3 trillion to $4 trillion. "What the debut offers is a read on demand for frontier AI exposure at scale and a public filing against which the business can now be measured," they say. Anthropic is up 15% to $95.82 after opening at $111.50 earlier. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

1350 ET - Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei tells CNBC he has remained calm about the company's initial public offering, even in spite of a challenging few weeks for the tech industry. He says he believes Anthropic's strong fundamentals are more important than how the market changes day to day, or even month to month. "We always want to underpromise and overdeliver," he says. His comments come after Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week, triggering a plunge in the stock. Before that, investors were selling-off AI-related stocks on concerns about overspending. Anthropic is up 16% to $96.61 after jumping to $111.50 when it opened for trading earlier. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

1302 ET - Markets remain caught between AI optimism on one side and Fed tightening on the other, writes Matthew Ryan, Head of Market Strategy at Ebury. Solid U.S. data and hawkish Fed rhetoric point to a December hike that is not only highly likely, but may be followed by further tightening in early 2027. "This is keeping the 10-year Treasury yield above 5% and limiting gains in equities," Ryan wrote. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1228 ET - Home sales fell in New York State in October, while inventory and prices continued to rise, the New York State Association of Realtors says. October saw closed sales fall 6.1% from October 2025 to 10,042 this year. Pending sales also dropped, from 10,003 homes under contract last year to 8,949 last month. Prices rose 1.8%, to $435,000, compared to $427,100 in October 2025. Inventory also saw a rise, with inventory across the state increasing nearly 14% compared to a year ago, the Association added. Median sales prices have now increased year-over-year in 38 of the last 39 months, the group added. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1137 ET - UBS expects business investment to contribute to Canada GDP growth next year and in 2028 — although it frames this as a gradual recovery after a prolonged period of lackluster spending. The firm says it anticipates new investment-related tax incentives to fuel some of the pickup, as well as higher energy prices as that persuades oil-and-gas producers to bolster spending. Trade uncertainty and higher borrowing costs could pose a notable headwind, UBS cautions. "This is a gradual recovery from a weak base rather than a sustained continuation of recent double-digit quarterly growth rates," says the firm, in reference to 2Q GDP data. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1134 ET - Palo Alto Networks delivered against a very high bar, Mizuho analysts say in a research note, posting sharply higher revenue in the recent quarter. "Meanwhile, Palo Alto meaningfully raised its FY27 revenue guide, and guided F2Q27 above as well," they write. The analysts remain bullish on Palo Alto's improving mix shift toward higher-growth recurring revenue. "We reiterate that Palo Alto clearly possesses the strongest array of cloud assets among traditional network security vendors," they write. Shares are up 6%. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

data.title: Washington outsources defense of transgender sports law to Bryan Cave
data.description:
By Mike Scarcella and David Thomas

The state of Washington turned to law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner after its voters adopted a ballot measure limiting transgender students' participation in school sports, marking the latest example of a state attorney general retreating from or avoiding direct involvement in defending a politically charged measure.

The Washington state law, Initiative 638, requires school districts and athletic organizations to prohibit “biologically male” students from competing in female-only athletic competitions in K-12 public school sports.

Voters in four US states approved ballot measures to restrict transgender rights in the midterm elections earlier this month, sending a warning to Democrats on an issue that has divided the party and is likely to remain a political challenge heading into the 2028 presidential race.

Bryan Cave will dedicate at least three partners to defend the new law, according to a contract obtained by Reuters through a public records request. The contract sets a maximum compensation of $150,000 but allows additional funds to be requested if necessary.

Speaking at an event in Chicago on Wednesday, Democratic Washington Attorney General ‌Nick Brown said the state has "taken a leadership position to defend the rights and dignity of all Washingtonians, including transgender people in our state." He said it could create a conflict if his office did not outsource its obligation to defend the law.

"I did not want to put our office in a position where some of those arguments and some of those positions that we have taken might be in conflict with this new law passed by the people," Brown said.

He said Bryan Cave, which has worked for the state in the past, has "a stellar representation" and will defend the law while "we continue to do the advocacy that we have always done over the last couple of years."

A Bryan Cave spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

State legislators in the past have appointed outside lawyers, or courts have approved an alternate plaintiff in disputes over reproductive rights, same-sex marriage and other politically divisive measures, allowing laws to be defended in court even when a state's top legal officer declines to take the case.

Former Democratic North Carolina governor and attorney general Roy Cooper, who recently won a US Senate race in the state, in 2016 declined to defend a state law that he said discriminates against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people. In 2018, Iowa's Democratic attorney general withdrew from defending a restrictive law targeting reproductive rights.

Some AGs have declined to enforce certain state laws entirely. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, told Reuters on Wednesday that she refused to prosecute any doctor or woman under a statewide abortion ban that was passed in 1864. Arizona repealed the law in 2024.

Bryan Cave's contract with Washington state shows Seattle office managing partner Erin Ehlert is on the team, in addition to partners Barbara Smith Tyson and Randall Thomsen. Smith Tyson is an appellate group co-leader. Thomsen is identified as lead counsel on the contract.

Smith Tyson will charge $950 an hour, Ehlert is billing at $850 and Thomsen will charge $828, the contract shows. They did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The St. Louis-founded firm first opened an office in Seattle in 2023, a few years after it merged with London's Berwin Leighton Paisner to form BCLP.

There's already at least one lawsuit against the new Washington state measure, filed by the state’s largest teachers union, a nonprofit that advocates for transgender kids and the parents of seven transgender students.

The American Civil Liberties Union's Washington office, which is representing the plaintiffs, declined to comment on Brown's appointment of an outside law firm.

The plaintiffs on Wednesday asked a judge to stop the law from taking effect on December 3.

LAW FIRMS ON TRACK FOR ANOTHER YEAR OF DOUBLE-DIGIT REVENUE GROWTH

Major US law firms are poised to see another year of double-digit revenue growth, thanks to rising billing rates and demand, new survey data released Wednesday by Wells Fargo showed.

Revenue for the 200 highest-grossing US law firms grew by 12.2% during the first months of 2026, according to Wells Fargo’s Legal Specialty Group. That’s a slight increase over the same period last year, when law firm revenue grew by 11.7%.

Law firm profitability was also up – net income increased by 15.8%, higher than the 14.4% growth Wells Fargo reported for the first nine months of 2025.

Wells Fargo also found that billing rates, a key revenue driver, continued to rise, along with overall demand for legal services.

Wells Fargo surveyed more than 120 law firms, including 68 of the 100 highest-grossing law firms.

ALSO ON BILLABLE HOURS' RADAR THIS WEEK...

-- The scattering of lawyers from Weil, Gotshal & Manges continues. Since Weil voted to dissolve the 95-year-old law firm, Cleary Gottlieb, Dechert, Kirkland & Ellis, Paul Hastings, Simpson Thacher and Skadden have added key partners or groups from the firm.

-- Keker, Van Nest & Peters said it will stop extending full-time job offers to its summer associates at the end of the summer, even as other law firms have been trying to recruit students who have only started their first semester of law school.
